title: Readmission program report (Simpson's paradox and friends)

items.text: Simpson's paradox: the program does worse within each risk tier (5.0% vs 4.0%, 25% vs 22%); the overall gap comes from enrolling mostly low-risk patients
paraphrases: Simpson's paradox: within both risk tiers the program group has a higher readmission rate.
Stratified by tier, the program looks worse (5.0% vs 4.0%; 25% vs 22%); the headline gap is driven by case mix.
The aggregate result reverses once you split by risk tier - program patients were 80% low risk vs 20% in comparison.

items.text: Selection bias: enrollment required answering the first call and agreeing, so the program group is systematically more reachable, engaged and healthier
paraphrases: Selection bias - only patients who picked up and agreed were enrolled, so they differ from the comparison group.
Self-selection: engaged, reachable patients are healthier on average, regardless of the calls.
The groups weren't randomized; enrollment depended on answering the first call.

items.text: Survivorship / per-protocol bias: 140 dropouts who didn't complete all 3 calls were removed from the program group only
paraphrases: The 140 patients who dropped out were removed from the program group - survivorship bias.
Only completers are analysed (per-protocol); an intention-to-treat analysis would keep the 140.
Removing people who left the program before 3 calls flatters the result.

items.text: Confounding by site: Northgate launched meds-to-beds in the same period and supplies 85% of program patients vs 40% of comparison
paraphrases: Confounder: Northgate's meds-to-beds service started at the same time, and 85% of program patients came from Northgate.
The improvement may be due to another intervention (bedside medication delivery) rather than the calls.
Site is a confounder - program patients are concentrated at Northgate (85% vs 40%).

items.text: Small samples and no uncertainty: the Spanish-language '100% reduction' is 2/10 vs 0/9, and no confidence intervals are given anywhere
paraphrases: The Spanish-language finding is 0 of 9 vs 2 of 10 - far too small to conclude anything.
No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any result.
A '100% reduction' on n=9 is noise; sample size is tiny.

items.text: Base-rate neglect: with 13% prevalence, 90% sensitivity and 70% specificity, only about 31% of flagged patients are readmitted, not 90%
paraphrases: Base-rate neglect: a flagged patient is not 90% likely to be readmitted; with 13% prevalence the PPV is about 31%.
The forecast confuses sensitivity with positive predictive value - most flagged patients are false positives.
With specificity 70% and a 13% base rate, roughly 2 of 3 flagged patients would never be readmitted anyway.
negatives: The 90% sensitivity of the risk model is impressive.

items.text: Metric definition change: from July, planned readmissions no longer count, and the program group is more concentrated after July (70% vs 50%)
paraphrases: Measure changed mid-period: from July only unplanned readmissions count, and 70% of program patients were discharged after July vs 50% of comparison.
The readmission definition changed on July 1, which mechanically lowers program rates.
Apples-to-oranges: program patients are mostly measured with the narrower 'unplanned' definition.

items.text: The forecast double-counts the effect: a 50% reduction is assumed although the within-tier data show no benefit, and it is applied to all flagged patients
paraphrases: The 5,400 forecast assumes a 50% effect that the stratified data don't support.
The expansion projection is inflated: it stacks an unsupported 50% reduction on a wrong 90% probability.
Extrapolating to all hospitals assumes the effect generalizes - it is overstated.

decoys.text: Readmissions to other hospitals are not captured
decoys.why_not: Readmissions come from the state all-payer claims database, which covers any hospital in the state.
paraphrases: Patients readmitted at other hospitals may be missed.
Readmission leakage to outside hospitals is not counted.
Only readmissions to our own partner hospitals are tracked.

decoys.text: Patients with multiple discharges may be double-counted
decoys.why_not: Only each patient's first 2025 discharge is used.
paraphrases: Same patient could appear multiple times - duplicates inflate counts.
Repeat discharges may be double-counted.
Risk of counting a patient twice across index admissions.

decoys.text: The groups may differ in age or sex
decoys.why_not: The report shows mean age 67 vs 68 and 54% vs 55% female.
paraphrases: Age differences between groups could confound the result.
The program group may be younger.
No adjustment for demographics such as sex or gender.
